newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Robusta producers vow curbs, trade sceptical.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Robusta producers vow curbs, trade sceptical.

text.p: Ivory Coast reiterated on Wednesday that an extra cut of 1.3 million 60-kg bags in coffee exports that was ageed by producer nations for the first half of 1997 would be implemented.
But this was greeted with scepticism by some participants in the trade.

The Ivorian Commodities Minister, Guy-Alain Gauze, also ruled out the possibility of the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) relaxing its quotas despite the rally in world prices since January.

Gauze told reporters he had a meeting with Rubens Barbosa, the Brazilian ambassador to the UK and the head of the ACPC, earlier on Wednesday and agreed that the additional cuts should be implemented "without any adjustments."

African robusta coffee growers, led by Ivory Coast, had spearheaded the idea of an extra cut to help lift robusta prices and narrow the huge differential with the premium arabica type of beans, grown mainly in Central and South America.
While both prices of arabicas, underpinned by tight supplies, and robusta have risen, the differential has failed to narrow.
It has risen to record high of $1.21 a lb from 51 cents in December and 27.1 cents in March last year.
"The arbitrage has succeeded in growing...this means that market does not believe (in the robusta export cuts) or it is not happening," said one European trader.
"There's no huge offtake in robusta. The coffee is 10 percent over-supplied," he said.
Backers of the ACPC plan said the scheme was justified as the current robusta coffee price of 80 cents a lb was still at a historically low level.
"It's a lousy price...it's not giving reasonable returns to the farmers," said one.
The ACPC has called a technical meeting for March 20 in London to discuss prices and supply and make recommendations to an ACPC council to be held in May.
The new cut of 1.3 million bags, agreed at a meeting of the 14-member ACPC in Rio de Janeiro on January, took projected group exports down to 24.98 million in the first six months of 1997.
The accord was to cut African exports by 850,000 bags. Indonesia will take the remaining 150,000 bags of the robusta share of one million.
Robusta prices on the London futures market were hovering at $1,740 a tonne on Wednesday after a rise to a new nine-month-peak of $1,825 overnight.
Prices are still sharply up from a January 7 low of $1,203.
Robusta, used mainly in soluble manufacture or in cheaper blends in many market, accounts for more than 30 percent of world production.
At the moment, robusta supplies are being met by Vietnam and African producers.
Indonesia, the largest robusta producer, is out of season but the main harvest is due from May. One trader said the first arrivals of Indonesian coffee will reach Europe by the second half of April.
"We are seeing larger volume from May," he said. Indonesia had a bumper crop of 7.5 million bags last season and traders said the yield could be slightly lower this season on crop cycle.
Analysts said the growing supply tightness of arabicas could be a blessing to robusta producers.

"Robusta producers may take comfort from the likelihood that as market prices rise there will be greater substitution in blends and they will gain accordingly," a veteran market analyst, Kerry Muir, wrote in an article published by German statistician F.O. Licht late last week. -- London newsroom +44 171 542 4985
